defaults.permitted_development: Across Lincolnshire, the standard fence and wall limits are 2 metres in most positions and 1 metre where the boundary is next to a highway used by vehicles. If the property is affected by listed-building controls, Article 4 restrictions or specific planning conditions, the ordinary householder route may not apply.

rules.height_rules: Across Lincolnshire, the usual boundary limits are 2 metres overall, or 1 metre where the enclosure sits next to a highway used by vehicles. A site that has been raised, terraced or fronted by a retaining wall can reach those limits faster than homeowners expect.
rules.depth_rules: Across Lincolnshire, depth is not usually the deciding measurement for fences and walls. The issue is more often whether the enclosure follows the normal boundary line or turns into a more substantial engineered structure with level changes behind it.
rules.boundary_rules: Across Lincolnshire, a fence or wall is easiest to keep within householder rights when it follows an ordinary residential boundary and does not block visibility at an access or corner. Heritage constraints can also apply where the boundary relates to listed buildings or historic frontages.
rules.roof_rules: Across Lincolnshire, a fence or wall is not judged on roof form, but the top treatment still matters. Copings, trellis panels, archways and taller gate piers can all change the effective height and appearance.
rules.materials_rules: Across Lincolnshire, material choice is not controlled in the same way as height, yet it still matters. A boundary that fits the character of the house and street will usually sit more comfortably than one with overly heavy or visually harsh materials on a prominent frontage.

restrictions.listed_building: Boundary works to or around a listed building can require listed building consent, especially where historic walls, railings, piers or gates are being altered or removed.

rules.permitted_development: In East Lindsey, a new fence, wall or gate at a house is usually permitted development up to 2 metres high, or up to 1 metre where it is next to a highway used by vehicles or the footpath of such a highway. The normal right falls away where listed-building controls, Article 4 directions or relevant planning conditions apply.

rules.height_rules: The main national height limits are 2 metres in most positions and 1 metre next to a highway used by vehicles. Height is measured from ground level, so raised beds, retaining walls or a sloping site can change the real planning answer.
rules.depth_rules: There is no separate depth allowance for fences and walls. What matters more is the line of the boundary, any change in ground level, and whether the structure starts to behave like retaining engineering rather than ordinary enclosure.
rules.boundary_rules: Boundary works that sit by a driveway, corner plot or junction still need safe visibility. The normal right is also restricted if the boundary adjoins a listed building or its curtilage, and demolition controls can matter in conservation areas.
rules.roof_rules: Fences and walls do not have a roof test, but cappings, trellis toppers, pergola-style additions or gates fixed to taller piers can all count toward the overall height and visual impact. Keep the whole boundary composition in mind rather than only the main panel height.
rules.materials_rules: There is no blanket requirement to copy the house materials, although front boundaries generally work better when the walling, railings or panels feel in scale with the street rather than engineered or overbearing.
